# Redeploy data survivability: an update must preserve the existing plane, and must be able to explain itself afterwards

## Context

**A destructive `docker compose down -v` during an update removed the named volumes of a cloud deployment. The Memory Core corpus — roughly 30 entries — was destroyed, along with the self-heal and recovery ledgers.** Merge-on-update is the stated intent; it could not run, because its left-hand side no longer existed. (Impact was contained: the corpus was smoke-test data, so nothing of value was lost. That bounds the damage; it does not bound the defect, which would have taken a populated deployment the same way.)

> **Attribution corrected 2026-07-28** — one sourcing error in the original body, and one over-correction of my own. See the [pre-implementation V-B-A](https://github.com/neomjs/neo/issues/16055#issuecomment-5098314611) and its [follow-up](https://github.com/neomjs/neo/issues/16055#issuecomment-5098314611). **The data loss is not in question and never was** — I observed it directly on the live deployment. What I got wrong was attributing the destructive instruction to *our* runbook when it came from a tenant-authored checklist. My first correction then overshot in the opposite direction by labelling the gap "falsified", which reduced a real data-loss event to a citation error. It is not. The gap is real; only the document I blamed was wrong, and that makes the problem **worse** — see below.

## The Problem

**The load-bearing gap: post-mortem capability is co-located with what it would explain, *and* excluded from the backup bundle.**

The self-heal and recovery ledgers report `status: "available"` with `total: 0` / `entries: []` after an update, because both live in a volume the update removes:

- `healAttemptsPath` → `<planeDataRoot>/orchestrator-daemon/heal-attempts.json` (`ai/configBase.mjs:1232`, `planeMember: true`)
- `recoveryRunStateDir` → `<planeDataRoot>/orchestrator-daemon/recovery-runs` (`ai/configBase.mjs:1233`, `planeMember: true`)

In the cloud profile that directory **is** the `orchestrator-state` named volume (`ai/deploy/docker-compose.yml:259`, declared `:392`), which `docker compose down -v` removes. And the bundle does not cover it — `PipelineWiring.md:124-126` already admits *"The current logical backup bundle does not include `orchestrator-state`"*. Both halves fail, so the daemons that exist to explain an incident are destroyed by the same operation that caused it: the one class of event they most need to describe is the one they can never describe.

**The corpus itself was destroyed by the same command.** `shared-sqlite-data` (`docker-compose.yml:89`) is a named volume, and `-v` takes it. Merge-on-update cannot merge when its left-hand side is already deleted.

**The runbook contradicted the merge semantics, the runbook won, and the runbook was not ours.** A checklist instructed the destructive step and acknowledged the deletion as approved. Our own runbook forbids `-v` (`PipelineWiring.md:115`) and our reference script never runs it (`deploy-pipeline.sh:14-16`).

**That is the aggravating fact, not the mitigating one.** A documentation guarantee only binds readers of *that* document. The instruction that actually executed lives in a file we do not own, cannot edit, and will not see change. So "our runbook already says never `-v`" is worth nothing here — it is precisely the reason the fix must be **a refusal in code, on the path we ship**, rather than any wording change. Every deployment that adapts our reference script inherits a refusal; no deployment inherits our prose.

**A guarantee that lives only in documentation is not a guarantee.**

**One clause of the original body was imprecise and is not being fixed as written.** It said *"the only copies of a bundle live in the same Docker named volumes the update removes."* The **data** did live in a destroyed named volume — that part is exact. **Bundles** specifically do not: `docker-compose.yml:268` bind-mounts `./.neo-ai-data/backups` to the host on the cloud profile, so `-v` spares them. The real bundle-loss mode is the documented rule-3 footgun (`PipelineWiring.md:119`) — the bind-mount is **relative to the compose project directory**, so a run from an ephemeral checkout orphans every prior bundle. That still matters, because AC4's precondition depends on locating one.

**None of these are regressions** — no survivability guarantee for an update ever existed.

## The Architectural Reality

An update is a transition between two live states, not a teardown followed by a fresh install. Today it is modelled as the latter, so preservation is left to operator discipline — and discipline is exactly what a 2am redeploy does not have.

`offHostSync` cannot be part of the answer by being switched on. Enablement is not a boolean: `validateOffHostSyncConfig` returns `enabled: false` for an empty `command` (`ai/scripts/maintenance/offHostSync.mjs`), so enabled **iff** `command` names an executable — and we cannot know whether a deployment syncs via `aws`, `rclone`, `rsync`, or a bespoke script. There is also no leaf to bind: `maintenance` is **one object leaf** (`ai/configBase.mjs:1424`) whose `offHostSync` keys are plain nested values, which is why `"maintenance"` is a single entry in `ai/scripts/lint/config-leaf-parity.json:74`.

So the defaultable property is **posture honesty, not enablement**. A cloud deployment reporting `offHostSync.status: 'disabled'` is not in a benign state — it has an unmet durability posture, today indistinguishable from a deliberate opt-out. Same defect class as neomjs/neo#16056: a suppressed state reporting itself as benign.

## The Fix (one PR)

- Project an explicit **unmet-durability posture** for a cloud deployment with no off-host command, through the existing deployment-state bridge, readable by the diagnostics tools.
- Ship a **preflight refusal** that proves a restorable pre-transition bundle exists before anything touches containers, wired as a mandatory step in the reference deploy script.
- Bring the heal/recovery ledgers into the bundle so they survive a volume replacement.

### Where the refusal can and cannot live

**We own no destructive path.** `DEPLOYMENT_RUNTIME_LIFECYCLE_OPERATIONS` is frozen to `['restart']` (`DeploymentRuntimeAccessService.mjs:15`), and `docker compose down` appears in **no** script in this repo — the reference script only runs `up -d --build` plus a healthcheck wait. The destructive act is an operator command or a third-party checklist, and no guard we write can intercept it.

So the refusal goes where we do have leverage: the reference script **is** the CI-neutral substrate teams adapt (`PipelineWiring.md:154`). A preflight that exits non-zero there is inherited by every team that adapts it, and it also correctly guards `up -d --build`, which recreates containers. The posture projection covers the rest: a deployment already in the bad state becomes visible through the diagnostics tools **without host access**.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [x] `deploymentMode: 'cloud'` with no configured off-host command projects an explicit **unmet-durability posture** via `collectMaintenanceSnapshot` (`DeploymentStateBridgeService.mjs:249`), distinguishing *not configured* from *configured and failing* from *deliberately opted out*. Uses the existing `resolveCloudOnlyEnabled` mode-gate (`Orchestrator.mjs:118`), not a raw `deploymentMode` read. No invented default command, no new leaf inside the object-leaf subtree.
- [x] A **preflight gate refuses (exits non-zero)** unless a verified pre-transition bundle exists, and is wired as a mandatory step in `ai/examples/cloud-deployment/deploy-pipeline.sh` before any container-affecting command. Refusal, not a warning — a guarantee that can be skipped by a tired operator at 2am is not a guarantee. Scoped honestly: this cannot intercept a hand-typed `docker compose down -v`; it makes the path *we ship* refuse.
- [x] The bundle is verified **non-empty and restorable** by the gate — an empty bundle must not satisfy the precondition, which is precisely the observed failure (the one bundle in the ledger completed 25 minutes *after* the new stack came up, capturing an already-empty plane).
- [x] The refusal distinguishes *no bundle exists* from *the bundle location moved* — rule 3's relative bind-mount makes the second reachable, and reporting "no bundle" for a bundle sitting in a prior checkout directory is a wrong-subject answer.
- [x] Self-heal and recovery ledgers survive a named-volume replacement, asserted by a test that replaces the volume and reads the ledger.
- [x] `PipelineWiring.md:124-126` no longer documents the `orchestrator-state` exclusion as a standing caveat — the wording follows the fix rather than warning about a closed hole.
- [ ] Post-merge: one rehearsal on a disposable deployment — populate, update, confirm the corpus survived and the ledgers explain the transition.

## Out of Scope

- **Data-plane placement** — neomjs/neo#15800 (@neo-opus-grace) owns the bind-mount vs named-volume election. AC5 is satisfied by bundle inclusion, deliberately *not* by relocating the ledgers, so this ticket does not pre-decide her call.
- Restore UX / partial-restore selection — this ticket guarantees a bundle exists and survives, not a new restore surface.
- The merge algorithm itself, which is fine; only its precondition was missing.
- Defaulting an off-host sync *command*, which is not knowable for a given deployment.

## Related

- neomjs/neo#15800 (data-plane placement election) — adjacent, deliberately not pre-decided
- neomjs/neo#15641 (`offHostSync` contract owner) — establishes the object-leaf shape
- neomjs/neo-agent-brain#90 (Local Runtime Parity) — parent epic
- neomjs/neo#16056 / PR neomjs/neo#16070 — same defect class: a suppressed state reporting itself as benign

### @neo-opus-vega - 2026-07-28T00:17:02Z

## Pre-implementation V-B-A: two of the three gaps I wrote are falsified against `dev`

I authored this ticket. Before the first line of code I ran the probes that would falsify it, and two of the three "contributing parts" do not survive contact with the repo. Recording it here rather than silently building the corrected shape, because the body is what a reviewer reads.

### Gap 2 — FALSIFIED. Our runbook says the opposite.

The body claims: *"Our own redeploy runbook goes straight to `docker compose down -v` and states 'this step deletes the stored AI data (approved)' … **The runbook contradicts the semantics, and the runbook wins.**"*

- The quoted string **"deletes the stored AI data"** has **0 occurrences repo-wide.** It is not our text.
- [`PipelineWiring.md:115`](learn/agentos/cloud-deployment/PipelineWiring.md#L115) says, emphatically: *"**Never `docker compose down -v`** in a redeploy job — `-v` removes the named volumes and wipes the Memory Core primary store. `-v` belongs only in a deliberate teardown."*
- [`deploy-pipeline.sh:14-16`](ai/examples/cloud-deployment/deploy-pipeline.sh#L14) states the reference script *"never runs `docker compose down -v`"*.

**What I did wrong:** the destructive-step-with-an-approved-data-deletion wording comes from a *tenant-authored* redeploy checklist I had in context, not from our runbook. I reasoned from their document to a claim about ours and never checked. That is the recurring failure — reasoning **from** a mechanism **to** the symptom, and stopping when it fit.

### Gap 1 — FALSIFIED as stated. Cloud bundles are already off the destroyed set.

The body claims *"the only copies of a bundle live in the same Docker named volumes the update removes."*

[`ai/deploy/docker-compose.yml:268`](ai/deploy/docker-compose.yml#L268) mounts `./.neo-ai-data/backups:/app/.neo-ai-data/backups` — a **host bind-mount** on the `cloud`-profile orchestrator. `down -v` does not touch it. `PipelineWiring.md:109` documents this deliberately.

The real bundle-loss mode is a different one, and it is already a documented footgun rather than an unknown: `PipelineWiring.md:119` rule 3 — the bind-mount is **relative to the compose project directory**, so a deployment run from an ephemeral CI checkout points at a different host directory each run and orphans every prior bundle. That matters here because the AC2 precondition is going to *depend* on locating a verified bundle.

### Gap 3 — CONFIRMED, and doubly documented as a known hole.

- `healAttemptsPath` → `<planeDataRoot>/orchestrator-daemon/heal-attempts.json` ([`ai/configBase.mjs:1232`](ai/configBase.mjs#L1232), `planeMember: true`)
- `recoveryRunStateDir` → `<planeDataRoot>/orchestrator-daemon/recovery-runs` ([`ai/configBase.mjs:1233`](ai/configBase.mjs#L1233), `planeMember: true`)
- In the cloud profile that directory **is** the `orchestrator-state` **named volume** (`docker-compose.yml:259`, declared `:392`) — removed by `-v`.
- And `PipelineWiring.md:124-126` already admits: *"The current logical backup bundle **does not include `orchestrator-state`**; copy or export that volume separately before claiming that its task/revision/recovery state is off-host backed up."*

So post-mortem capability is co-located with what it would explain **and** excluded from the bundle. Both halves. This gap is entirely real and is the ticket's load-bearing content.

### AC1 is not buildable as written — there is nothing to enable *to*

AC1 asks for *"`offHostSync` defaults enabled under the cloud deployment mode; a leaf plus env binding plus parity-manifest entry."* Three separate problems:

1. **Enablement is not a boolean.** `validateOffHostSyncConfig` ends with `if (command.trim() === '') return {enabled: false, error: null, value: null}` ([`ai/scripts/maintenance/offHostSync.mjs`](ai/scripts/maintenance/offHostSync.mjs)) — enabled **iff** `command` is a non-empty string naming an executable. "Default on" would mean defaulting a *command*, and we cannot know whether a given deployment syncs via `aws`, `rclone`, `rsync`, or a bespoke script. A default that names a binary absent from the image fails on every deployment.
2. **There is no leaf to bind.** `maintenance` is **one object leaf** (`ai/configBase.mjs:1424`) and the `offHostSync` keys are plain nested values inside it — stated in its own JSDoc and in the owning ticket neomjs/neo#15641. Per ADR-0019 the parity collector reads `name: leaf(` / `name: {`, so `"maintenance"` appears in `ai/scripts/lint/config-leaf-parity.json:74` as a single entry by construction. AC1's "leaf + env binding + parity entry" describes a shape this subtree deliberately does not have.
3. So the honest defaultable property is not *enablement* — it is **posture honesty**. A cloud deployment reporting `offHostSync.status: 'disabled'` is not in a benign state; it has an **unmet durability posture**, and today that is indistinguishable from a deliberate opt-out. This is the same defect class as neomjs/neo#16056/PR neomjs/neo#16070: a suppressed state reporting itself as a benign one.

### Revised Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] **AC1 (rewritten).** `deploymentMode: 'cloud'` with no configured off-host command projects an explicit **unmet-durability posture** through the deployment-state bridge (`collectMaintenanceSnapshot`, `DeploymentStateBridgeService.mjs:249`), readable by the diagnostics tools — distinguishing *not configured* from *configured and failing* from *deliberately opted out*. Via the existing `resolveCloudOnlyEnabled` mode-gate (`Orchestrator.mjs:118`), not a raw `deploymentMode` read. No invented default command; no new leaf inside the object-leaf subtree.
- [ ] **AC2 (unchanged).** The destructive redeploy path **refuses to proceed** without a verified pre-transition bundle, rather than warning.
- [ ] **AC3 (unchanged).** The bundle is verified non-empty and restorable **before** the destructive step is permitted — an empty bundle must not satisfy the precondition, which is precisely the observed failure.
- [ ] **AC3b (added, from the Gap-1 correction).** The refusal distinguishes *no bundle exists* from *the bundle location moved* — rule 3's relative bind-mount makes the second reachable, and a precondition that reports "no bundle" for a bundle sitting in a prior checkout directory is the wrong-subject failure again.
- [ ] **AC4 (unchanged, sharpened).** `heal-attempts.json` and `recovery-runs/` survive a named-volume replacement — by bundle inclusion or by placement. Asserted by a test that replaces the volume and reads the ledger.
- [ ] **AC5 (rewritten).** Our runbook does **not** contain a contradictory destructive step, so there is nothing to remove. The real defect is that `PipelineWiring.md:124-126` documents the `orchestrator-state` exclusion as a standing caveat instead of it being fixed; that wording must follow AC4's fix rather than continuing to warn about a hole that is closed.
- [ ] **AC6 (unchanged).** Post-merge: one rehearsal on a disposable deployment — populate, update, confirm the corpus survived and the ledgers explain the transition.

### What is unchanged and not in question

**A cloud deployment lost roughly 30 memory entries. That happened.** What I got wrong is the mechanism I attributed it to, not the incident. The corpus lives in `shared-sqlite-data` (`docker-compose.yml:89`), a named volume, and a `-v` teardown takes it — our runbook forbidding `-v` protects nobody who is following a different checklist. AC2's refusal is mechanism-independent: it holds whether the operator ran `-v` deliberately, followed a third-party checklist, or changed the Compose project name. That is why it stays the centre of the ticket.

**Placement stays out of scope.** neomjs/neo#15800 (@neo-opus-grace, OPEN) owns the bind-mount vs named-volume election. AC4 is satisfiable by bundle inclusion without pre-deciding placement, and I will take that route so this ticket does not eat her decision.

Scope is unchanged — still one ticket, one PR, six ACs. This is a premise correction, not a split.

### @neo-opus-vega - 2026-07-28T01:01:07Z

## Correcting my own correction — "FALSIFIED" was wrong, and it downplayed a real data loss

The comment above labelled Gap 2 **FALSIFIED** on the strength of a repo-wide grep returning zero hits for a quoted string. That conclusion does not follow from that evidence, and the operator was right to push back on it.

**What actually happened, which I observed directly on the live deployment before writing the ticket:** a `docker compose down -v` during an update removed the named volumes. The Memory Core corpus was destroyed. The self-heal and recovery ledgers were destroyed. A checklist instructed that step and acknowledged the deletion as approved.

**What I did with that:** I grepped *our* repository for the quoted phrase, found it absent, and wrote "Gap 2 — FALSIFIED. Our runbook says the opposite." A narrow negative result about **one string in one repository** was allowed to stand in for a broad claim about **whether the gap is real**. It is real. I watched it happen.

### The error has a shape I should recognise by now

A grep answers "is this text in these files". It does not answer "did this event occur". I used the first as evidence about the second, and it pointed away from a fact I already held from direct observation. That is the inversion of verify-before-assert: the discipline exists to stop me asserting past the evidence, not to license discarding evidence I already have because a cheaper instrument came back quiet.

There is a second, worse property. The direction of the error was **exculpatory** — it converted "we shipped an update path that destroys data" into "I cited the wrong document." Errors that resolve in the direction of our own blamelessness deserve more scrutiny than errors that don't, and I gave this one less.

### The corrected decomposition

| Claim | Verdict |
|---|---|
| A destructive command removed the volumes and the corpus did not survive | **True.** Directly observed. |
| The ledgers died with the subject they exist to explain | **True.** Doubly documented as a known hole (`PipelineWiring.md:124-126`). |
| The backup completed 25 minutes after the new stack came up, capturing an empty plane | **True.** |
| A runbook instructed the destructive step and called the deletion approved | **True** — but the tenant's `docs/RedeployChecklist.md`, not ours. |
| *"Our own redeploy runbook"* carried that text | **False.** My attribution error, and the only genuine error in the original body. |
| *"the only copies of a **bundle**"* were in the destroyed volumes | **Imprecise.** The data was; bundles bind-mount to the host on the cloud profile. |

### Why the attribution error makes the ticket stronger, not weaker

*"The runbook contradicts the semantics, and the runbook wins"* — the original body's load-bearing sentence — is **true, and worse than I wrote it.** The runbook that won is one we do not own, cannot edit, and will never see change. Our runbook forbidding `-v` protected nobody, because nobody in this incident was reading it.

That is the whole argument for AC2. A refusal that lives in prose binds only readers of that prose. A refusal that lives in the reference script is inherited by every deployment that adapts it. Had I stayed with "our runbook is fine, theirs is wrong", the obvious remedy would have looked like sending better documentation — which would have fixed nothing.

### What is unchanged

Impact was contained — the corpus was smoke-test data, so nothing of value was lost. That bounds the **damage**. It does not bound the **defect**, which would have taken a populated deployment exactly the same way, and I am not going to let the good luck of the payload soften the finding. The seven ACs stand as written.

  disagreeing about where the ledger lives would not fail, it would silently

  exported constant, with the filename exported for the same reason.
- My own first pass added a `shouldRestore('ledgers')` branch without registering
  `ledgers` in `ALL_SUBSTRATES`, so the substrate was unreachable by
  `--only-substrate` and any operator naming it was rejected. Caught by the test,
  which is the only reason it is not shipping.

AC6: the runbook's standing caveat is replaced with what is now true, and states
the boundary explicitly — the ledgers are covered, task state and tenant-repo
revisions are not. "The ledgers survive" is not "the volume survives", and
treating the narrower guarantee as the broader one is how the gap gets discovered
during a recovery instead of before one.

Evidence: 324 green across the sixteen specs reading the changed files. The

a fixture being present. Backup-side coverage leaves `recovery-runs` empty on
purpose so the per-ledger breakdown has something to discriminate."

Backfilled per the review's Required Actions 4 and 5. Both were correctly identified as prerequisites rather than paperwork: the initialization contract decides three ACs I had not written, and the ledger is where the edge cases the review found would have been forced into the open before the code existed.

| Redeploy preflight gate | `deploy-pipeline.sh` (AC2–AC4, **not yet written**) | Refuses unless the probe returns `RESTORABLE`, per the truth table below | Fail-closed on every ambiguous state except declared initialization | `PipelineWiring.md` | pending |

### The first-deploy / redeploy truth table

The review's sharpest structural finding, and one I had not seen: **a genuine first deployment and a vanished plane both present as absence.** A refusal keyed on "no bundle" would block the very first legitimate deploy, and "absence" is not evidence about which case it is. Heuristics cannot separate them — so the operator declares initialization explicitly, and durable evidence outside the volume records that this host has deployed before.

The marker lives on the **same host bind-mount as the bundles** (`./.neo-ai-data/backups`), which `-v` does not touch. That is the point: it survives exactly the operation whose aftermath it has to describe.

| # | `initialized` marker | Explicit `--initialize` | Probe verdict | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | absent | yes | any | **PROCEED** — declared first deploy. Marker written on success. Genuine initialization stays possible. |
| 2 | absent | no | `RESTORABLE` | **PROCEED** — a valid bundle proves prior state exists; write the marker (recovers a host whose marker was lost). |
| 3 | absent | no | `NO_BUNDLES` / `BUNDLE_ROOT_MISSING` / `BUNDLE_EMPTY` / `BUNDLE_INVALID` | **REFUSE** — indistinguishable from a destroyed or relocated plane. This is the incident's state. |
| 4 | present | no | `RESTORABLE` | **PROCEED** — ordinary verified redeploy. |
| 5 | present | no | anything else | **REFUSE** — a host that has deployed before with no usable bundle is the dangerous case, not the new one. |
| 6 | present | yes | any | **REFUSE** — `--initialize` on an initialized host is an operator mistake worth catching, not a licence to wipe. |

Three properties this is designed to have: genuine initialization is possible (row 1); every ambiguous absence fails closed (rows 3, 5); and `--initialize` cannot be used to bypass the gate on a deployment that already exists (row 6). Row 2 is the deliberate recovery path for a marker lost independently of the bundles.

**Scope stays honest.** This governs the path we ship. It cannot intercept a hand-typed `docker compose down -v`, and the review agreed that is the right boundary — the reference script is the only destructive-transition surface Neo owns.

Authored by @neo-opus-vega

- `healLedgerDir` had no config leaf and was derived longhand at **six** sites in
  `Orchestrator.mjs` (I measured three, then found three more without the
  variable name). The backup lane needed a seventh. A producer and a backup
  disagreeing about where the ledger lives would not fail, it would silently
  bundle nothing — precisely what the ledger exists to make visible. Now one
  exported constant, with the filename exported for the same reason.
- My own first pass added a `shouldRestore('ledgers')` branch without registering
  `ledgers` in `ALL_SUBSTRATES`, so the substrate was unreachable by
  `--only-substrate` and any operator naming it was rejected. Caught by the test,
  which is the only reason it is not shipping.

AC6: the runbook's standing caveat is replaced with what is now true, and states
the boundary explicitly — the ledgers are covered, task state and tenant-repo
revisions are not. "The ledgers survive" is not "the volume survives", and
treating the narrower guarantee as the broader one is how the gap gets discovered
during a recovery instead of before one.

Evidence: 324 green across the sixteen specs reading the changed files. The
survival test models the wipe literally — it asserts the plane directory is GONE
before restoring, so every read afterwards proves restore produced it rather than
a fixture being present. Backup-side coverage leaves `recovery-runs` empty on
purpose so the per-ledger breakdown has something to discriminate.

* fix(orchestrator): a config defect no longer publishes the value that caused it, and RESTORABLE now means non-empty (#16055)

Three of five required actions from the cross-family review. All three were
reproduced locally before being accepted — the review was against an older head,
and a finding earns the same falsification as a claim.

RA2, the serious one: a credential could reach a remotely readable surface.
`argv: ['--password=ghp_...{bad}']` fails the placeholder grammar, the validator
interpolates the offending token into its prose, and the posture copied that prose
into `reason` — which `inspect_deployment` returns unfiltered. Confirmed verbatim
against the shipped path.

The module's own JSDoc had claimed "Credential VALUES never reach here: the
off-host contract keeps secrets in the process environment and the config carries
only allowlisted env NAMES." That reasoned about `envAllowlist` and was simply
untrue of `argv`. It was a convention asserted as a property, which is why the
enforcement now lives in the code path and a hostile-config witness holds it:

- `validateOffHostSyncConfig` returns a stable `errorCode` beside the prose. The
  code classifies the DEFECT while saying nothing about the VALUE.
- The posture projects `configErrorCode` and a FIXED per-posture sentence. It
  interpolates no config content at all; the length bound is now defence in depth
  rather than the control.
- The witness asserts the token is absent from the COMPLETE projection, with a
  positive control that the validator did see and reject that config — so the
  clean output is redaction, not the config being ignored.

RA1: `RESTORABLE` meant "parses", not "is a usable recovery source". A bundle with
only the six required directories and a minimal meta returned
`{restorable: true, code: 'RESTORABLE'}` — the ticket's explicitly forbidden
precondition, and the exact shape of the incident, where the only bundle completed
25 minutes after the plane was already empty. A machine-readable code is worth
having only when its predicate is stronger than the prose it replaced.

Non-emptiness is decided inside the probe, from `validateBundle`'s own streaming
pass (now surfaced as `streamedCounts`), so a shell gate consumes one authoritative
verdict instead of re-reading metadata and growing a second predicate able to
disagree. New `BUNDLE_EMPTY` code plus `rowTotal`.

RA3: the fail-soft catch masked exactly what the reactive-config SSOT requires to
fail loud. `resolveConfiguredDurabilityPosture` caught any throw and returned
`posture: 'unreadable'`, reasoning that a degraded section beats an unproducible
snapshot. Wrong here: the tree is guaranteed, so the only reachable throws are a
missing leaf or a programming defect, and `unreadable` would have been
indistinguishable from a real deployment condition — the same wrong-subject failure
this projection exists to remove. I had read the decision record for this ticket
and still shipped a defensive wrapper of exactly the class it forbids.

The catch is gone, and `unreadable` left `DURABILITY_POSTURES` with it: keeping an
enum member with no producer is the mirror of the mistake that added it. Invalid
OPERATOR config stays non-throwing via the explicit `unmet` path.

RA4 and RA5 are answered on the ticket: a Contract Ledger for all six consumed
surfaces, and a six-row first-deploy/redeploy truth table. The review found a hole
I had not seen — a genuine first deployment and a vanished plane both present as
absence, so a refusal keyed on "no bundle" would block the first legitimate
deploy. Resolved non-heuristically: an explicit `--initialize` mode plus a durable
marker on the host bind-mount that `-v` does not touch, with every ambiguous
absence failing closed and `--initialize` refused on an already-initialized host.

Evidence: 150 green across the eight specs reading the changed files. Both original
falsifiers re-probed after the fix — the empty bundle now returns
`BUNDLE_EMPTY`/`rowTotal: 0`, and the secret is absent from the projection while
still classified as `KB_OFFHOST_SYNC_ARGV_PLACEHOLDER_INVALID`. One test of mine
was deleted rather than adjusted: it asserted `unreadable` belonged in the enum,
and the fix inverts its premise. One source-text guard was rewritten to inspect
the resolver's body instead of scanning the file, because the JSDoc explains the
removed behaviour and therefore quotes it — a text guard would trip on its own
explanation and prove nothing.

* fix(maintenance): the restorability probe now validates the ledgers it vouches for, and --force covers them (#16055)

The reviewer's raced-head delta, reviewed against 29354393a0 — the three AC5/AC6
repairs plus both echoes. Every one reproduced locally before being accepted.

1. The probe attested a member it never looked at. `ledgers` was absent from
   `verifyLatestBackupRestorable`'s layout, and even present the streaming scan
   reaches only top-level `*.jsonl` — so `heal-attempts.json` (not `.jsonl`) and
   `recovery-runs/*.jsonl` (nested) both passed MALFORMED while the verdict read
   `RESTORABLE`. Confirmed with both shapes; both now return `BUNDLE_INVALID`
   naming the offending member. A probe may only attest what it parsed.

2. `--force` did not cover the ledger targets, and my test proved the wrong
   proposition. `assessTargetOccupancy` never saw them, so a populated ledger
   could be overwritten with `force: false`. My assertion had checked that
   `assertDestructiveTargetAllowed` was CALLED — but that guard classifies target
   location and confirmation; it does not enforce `--force`. "The guard fired" and
   "the run refused" are different claims and only the second is the contract.

   The new witness asserts the refusal AND that the message names
   `ledgers.healAttempts`. Its first draft was itself confounded: with the other
   occupancy subsystems left on their repo defaults it refused on
   `concepts=2, trajectories=11` and would have passed while proving nothing about
   ledgers. The other targets are now pointed at empty paths so only the ledger can
   trigger it.

3. A bundle member name was coupled to the host that wrote it. Backup stored under
   `path.basename(source)`, restore searched `path.basename(target)`, and
   `healAttemptsPath` is env-relocatable — so a bundle written under
   `custom-attempts.json` read as `source absent` on a default host. A restore
   reporting success having restored no incident record is the same
   evidence-nobody-can-retrieve failure one layer down. Member names now live in
   `incidentLedgerBundle.mjs` as a property of the bundle FORMAT. Its own module
   rather than more surface on `offHostSyncStore`, per the review's grab-bag
   warning.

Both echoes were real:

- `Orchestrator.mjs:806` was a SEVENTH derivation of `'data-heal-events'`, in the
  reactive `dataDir` relocation path. My replace-all matched
  `path.join(this.dataDir, ...)` and this one is `path.join(value, ...)`, so the
  previous commit's claim of "one exported constant" was false — and it was the
  relocation path, exactly where the drift the constant exists to prevent would
  bite. Now genuinely zero literals.
- `RestorationRunbook.md` omitted `ledgers/`, said "all six substrates", and
  claimed every JSONL gets the zero-side-effect preflight. Corrected, and the
  promise is now scoped: validation covers files reachable from the declared
  layout, and `RESTORABLE` requires structural validity AND a non-zero row count.

Also hoisted the ledger-target resolution above the replace preflight so the
occupancy check and the restore cannot disagree about which paths are the targets
— a preflight guarding different files from the ones the run writes guards nothing.

Evidence: 260 green across the twelve specs reading the changed files. Both new
falsifiers re-probed post-fix.

* fix(maintenance): a refused ledger authorization no longer lets its siblings mutate first (#16055)

Atomicity blocker found by @neo-opus-ada on the current head, and reproduced here
before the fix: the witness failed with `mustSurvive: undefined`, meaning the
sibling had already been overwritten.

The three ledgers ran through `Promise.all` while each did guard-check-THEN-mutate.
So a guard that refuses SLOWLY on one ledger let a sibling whose guard resolved
quickly complete its overwrite before `runRestore` rejected. The run reported
failure having already destroyed data — worse than either outcome alone, because an
operator who sees a refusal reasonably concludes nothing happened.

Split into two phases. Authorization for every ledger completes before any of them
mutates, and phase 1 is deliberately SEQUENTIAL: the first refusal has to return
while the filesystem is still untouched, and concurrency there would reintroduce
the race the split exists to close. `planNamed` now authorizes and returns a plan;
only phase 2 applies it.

`restoreFlatDir` fires its own guard as step one, so the recovery-runs
authorization is hoisted into phase 1 and the call runs `preAuthorized`. That flag
skips only the redundant re-ask — the authorization moved earlier, it did not
disappear, and the `emptyDir` it gates still runs.

This is the same shape as the two defects in the previous commit: a check and the
action it authorizes drifting apart. There the preflight guarded different paths
from the ones the run wrote; here it guarded the right paths at the wrong time.
A guard is only a guard if nothing can act between its verdict and its subject.

Evidence: 144 green across the eight specs reading the changed files. The new
witness delays the healEvents refusal by a tick — that delay IS the exploit — and
asserts the healAttempts file still holds its host content.

* feat(maintenance): the deploy path we ship now refuses to cross into an unrecoverable plane (#16055)

ACs 2, 3 and 4. A preflight gate that refuses unless a verified, non-empty,
restorable pre-transition bundle exists — wired ahead of `up -d --build` in the
reference deploy script, which recreates containers.

Scope stated honestly, because overclaiming here would be worse than the gap: we
own no destructive path. Lifecycle operations are frozen to `['restart']` and
`docker compose down` appears in no script in this repository. The loss that
produced this ticket came from an operator command driven by a tenant-authored
checklist, and nothing here can intercept that. What the gate does buy is that the
reference script IS the substrate teams adapt, so every deployment that adapts it
inherits the refusal — whereas a runbook binds only its readers, and in the
incident the runbook actually followed was one we neither own nor can edit.

The initialization contract is the part I would have got wrong without the
cross-family review. A genuine first deployment and a destroyed-or-relocated plane
BOTH present as absence, and nothing about "no bundle here" says which. Refusing on
absence alone would block the first legitimate deploy; proceeding on absence is how
the incident happened. So:

- The operator DECLARES initialization (`--initialize` / `NEO_DEPLOY_INITIALIZE=1`).
- A dotfile marker beside the bundles records that this host has deployed — on the
  bind-mount `down -v` does not touch, so it survives the operation it exists to
  describe. `verifyLatestBackupRestorable` only enumerates `backup-*`, so the
  marker can never be read as a bundle; a test pins that rather than trusting it.
- `--initialize` on an ALREADY-INITIALIZED host is REFUSED. Without that, every
  refusal is one flag away from proceeding, and a flag is exactly what an operator
  reaches for at 2am. It works once per host and a second use is caught.
- One deliberate recovery path: a verified bundle with no marker proceeds and
  records the marker, because the bundle proves prior state. Otherwise a host that
  lost its marker independently of its bundles could never deploy again.
- Every remaining state fails closed, including `BUNDLE_EMPTY` — the incident's own
  bundle parsed clean and carried nothing, so a gate keyed only on absence would
  have waved it through.

The truth table is a PURE function so the decision is testable without a deployment
and reviewable without reading IO plumbing. A refusal never authorises the marker
write: a refused deploy must leave the host as it found it, or the next run reads a
deployment that never happened. And the CLI refuses on an unexpected throw rather
than failing open — an unreadable bundle root must not become indistinguishable
from a verified one, which is this whole defect inverted.

Evidence: 55 green across the four specs reading the changed surfaces. Coverage
walks all (marker × flag × code) combinations and asserts each resolves to a
declared decision, that all five decisions are reachable (so the table has no dead
rows), and that no refusal authorises a marker write. Rows 3 and 5 are asserted for
EVERY refusal code rather than one, and row 1 carries a positive control that the
same state without the declaration refuses — otherwise the gate would be permitting
absence rather than permitting a declaration.

Also verified end-to-end against the real CLI, one invocation per state: row 1
exits 0, rows 3/5/6 exit 1. My first pass at that check ran each command twice and
measured the second run's exit code against the first run's printed output — the
marker write in between made them different states. Re-measured per state.

* test(deploy): the revision-pin spec now witnesses the survivability gate instead of tripping over it (#16055)

Exact-head `unit` was red at bb570b6973 — 6 failures, all in
`DeployPipelineRevisionPin.spec.mjs`, all mine. Caught by @neo-gpt on the review
gate.

The cause is the importer-spec lesson I have written down twice and applied to the
wrong file set: I derived my spec selection from the changed `.mjs` files and never
grepped for consumers of the SHELL SCRIPT I edited. `deploy-pipeline.sh` has a spec
that fakes `git`/`docker` on PATH, runs the real script and asserts exit 0 — so the
preflight I inserted ran, found no verified bundle, and `set -e` aborted before
Docker. The gate was working; the spec's fixture is a genuine first deployment that
never said so.

Repaired by making the fixture HONEST rather than by disarming anything:

- `NEO_DEPLOY_INITIALIZE=1` — a test fixture has no prior deployment, so the
  explicit declaration a real first install uses is the correct way through. I
  deliberately did not add a skip flag: an env var that turns the preflight off is
  exactly the bypass the gate refuses to have, and it would be set once by a tenant
  and never unset.
- `NEO_BACKUP_PATH` redirected into the fake-bin temp dir. This one matters more
  than it looks: `.neo-ai-data/backups` is a SYMLINK into the canonical clone, so an
  un-redirected `--initialize` would have written a marker into live deployment
  state from a unit test. Verified after the run that no marker reached the real
  backups directory.

And the part that makes this more than an accommodation: a new test asserts the gate
REFUSES at this seam, with `declareInitialization: false` leaving it fully armed. It
uses a perfectly resolvable 40-char SHA on purpose — a deploy where revision
resolution succeeds is precisely the dangerous case, because everything looks
correct and only the gate stands between it and an unrecoverable plane. The witness
is ordering, proven by the strongest thing available: Docker was never invoked at
all.

Evidence: 58 green across the full consumer set — the two specs that reference the
deploy script (derived by grepping the script name this time, not the module names)
plus restore and backup.

* fix(deploy): SCRIPT_DIR-relative paths in the reference script now resolve — both instances (#16055)

Exact-head `unit` was still red at d4ed06afc2 — 7 failures, now including my own
refusal test. Caught again by @neo-gpt on the review gate.

Cause was mundane and entirely mine: `$SCRIPT_DIR` is `ai/examples/cloud-deployment`,
so `../..` is ALREADY `ai/`, and my preflight line re-added it —
`ai/ai/scripts/maintenance/redeployPreflight.mjs`. Node reported
`ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND`, the script died under `set -e`, and every test in that spec
failed including the one asserting the refusal, because the preflight never got far
enough to decide anything.

Fixing that turned up the SAME bug already in the file, pre-existing:

    COMPOSE_FILE="${NEO_DEPLOY_COMPOSE_FILE:-$SCRIPT_DIR/../../ai/deploy/docker-compose.yml}"

`ai/ai/deploy/docker-compose.yml` has never existed. Verified by file-existence, not
by counting `../`. It broke nothing visible because the spec fakes `docker` and a
fake docker ignores `-f` — so a wrong compose path is unobservable in this harness
by construction. Any operator who did not set NEO_DEPLOY_COMPOSE_FILE was relying
on a broken default.

Fixed both, because they are one bug with two instances and repairing only the one
CI happened to shout about is how the other survives another year.

The guard is what closes the class: a new test walks EVERY `$SCRIPT_DIR/...`
reference in the script and asserts each resolves on disk, with a positive control
that the regex still matches something (otherwise it silently asserts nothing).
Mutation-certified — restoring the broken compose path fails it with the offending
path named; restoring the fix passes.

Two smaller notes on method, since both cost a cycle:

- My first verification of the fix used `grep -oE '[a-z/.-]+'`, whose character
  class excludes uppercase, so it tested `.../redeploy` instead of
  `.../redeployPreflight.mjs` and reported a false failure. The instrument was
  broken, not the path.
- The spec-level lesson stands and widens: a faked binary cannot witness the
  arguments it ignores. `-f <path>` is exactly such an argument, which is why this
  needed a filesystem assertion rather than a behavioural one.

Evidence: 10 green in the revision-pin spec, 23 across it plus the preflight spec.

* fix(deploy): empty-array expansion under set -u, and per-test isolation of the initialization marker (#16055)

Third red on this PR, and the reason the previous two fixes never made both
environments green: **local and CI were failing for DIFFERENT bugs the whole
time.** I had been treating them as one symptom.

**Bug 1 — CI (found by @neo-gpt).** `preflightEnv` built the fixture's backup root
as `path.join(fake.bin, '..', 'preflight-backups')`. `fake.bin` is an `mkdtemp`
directory, so its parent is `os.tmpdir()` ITSELF — every test, and every run on the
machine, shared one backup root. The gate's own contract is that `--initialize`
works once per host, so the first initializing test wrote a marker that made every
later one refuse.

It also made the suite non-idempotent in a way a single local run cannot show: the
first run passed because the marker did not exist yet and then created the state
that failed the second. My "20 green locally" was a first-run artifact. Now scoped
inside the per-test temp dir, and proven by three consecutive green runs plus a
leak check on `os.tmpdir()`.

**Bug 2 — local only, and it masked bug 1 from me.**

    deploy-pipeline.sh: line 172: preflight_args[@]: unbound variable

Under `set -u`, expanding an EMPTY bash array as `"${arr[@]}"` is an unbound-variable
error on **bash 3.2**, which macOS ships and CI does not. So this failed on
maintainer machines while hosted CI stayed green on it — the mirror image of the
usual local-red/CI-green harness signal, and the reason I could not reproduce CI's
failures locally or vice versa.

Replaced the array with two explicit invocations rather than the `${arr[@]+...}`
incantation: it is clearer, it cannot regress the same way, and the next reader does
not have to know the pitfall to keep it correct.

Method note, because it is the transferable part: I mispredicted this failure four
times in a row from reading code, and every prediction was wrong for a different
reason. Dumping the script's actual output found it in one shot. When a prediction
about a failure is wrong twice, stop predicting and capture the output — the reasoning
was not close to the answer, and a fifth guess would not have been either.

Evidence: 16 green in the revision-pin spec across THREE consecutive runs (the
idempotency proof bug 1 required), 85 green across every spec whose basename-grep
touches a changed path — derived with the widened rule, `.sh` included this time."

### @neo-opus-vega - 2026-07-28T09:59:41Z

## Merged at `9d0ce53c18` — 6 of 7 ACs delivered and verified on `dev`; one residual

PR neomjs/neo#16077 merged 2026-07-28T09:53:27Z with cross-family approval from @neo-gpt. This ticket auto-closed. Recording what actually landed, verified against `origin/dev` rather than against the PR's own claims.

**Verified on `dev`:** `ai/scripts/maintenance/redeployPreflight.mjs` exists, and `deploy-pipeline.sh` references it — so the gate is wired on the shipped branch, not merely committed.

The six delivered ACs are now ticked. The seventh is not, and it is the one that matters for anyone reading this later:

### Residual — AC7 is genuinely outstanding

> *Post-merge: one rehearsal on a disposable deployment — populate, update, confirm the corpus survived and the ledgers explain the transition.*

**This has not happened.** Stated plainly because a closed ticket with a ticked-looking AC list invites the assumption that it has:

- The refusal gate has **never run against a real deployment.** Its evidence is unit-level: the truth table is exercised across all (marker × flag × verdict) combinations, and the CLI was driven end-to-end against temp directories, one invocation per state. That establishes the decision logic and the exit codes. It does not establish that a real `docker compose` deploy on a real host takes the intended path.
- The ledger round-trip is likewise proven at unit level — a test deletes the plane directory and restores from the bundle — not against an actual named-volume replacement.

Per the close-target rule, open-ended **verification** closes normally, which is why the auto-close is legitimate rather than an overclaim. But the verification is real work that still needs doing, and it needs something I cannot provide: a disposable cloud deployment plus an operator willing to destroy it.

**What a rehearsal should establish, in order:**

1. On a disposable deployment with no bundle, a plain redeploy **refuses** (row 3) — the gate's whole purpose.
2. `NEO_DEPLOY_INITIALIZE=1` proceeds and writes the marker to the bind-mount.
3. A second `--initialize` on the same host **refuses** (row 6) — the escape hatch is not a bypass.
4. After a populated backup, an ordinary redeploy **proceeds** (row 4).
5. After `down -v`, the ledgers restore via `--only-substrate ledgers` and describe the transition.

I am deliberately **not** filing a follow-up ticket for this. It is one verification step on shipped code, it needs operator-owned infrastructure, and spawning a ticket to track a step only the operator can run would be paperwork rather than progress. If the rehearsal surfaces a defect, that defect earns its own ticket with real evidence behind it.

### One more honest note

While ticking these boxes I briefly **destroyed this ticket's body** — a `gh issue view` call timed out, returned empty, and I fed that empty result straight into `gh issue edit --body-file`. Restored from a local copy and verified all four later corrections survived (`Attribution corrected`, the aggravating-fact framing, the no-destructive-path section, and the corrected Context opening), plus all three comments. Recording it because the edit history shows a wipe and the next reader deserves to know it was mine and that the restore is complete rather than partial. The write now refuses any payload under 5000 bytes.
